claims.claim: Both Adam Smith and Karl Marx shared the modern public contempt for unproductive labor, treating it as parasitical and noting that menial servants leave nothing behind in return for their consumption.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Moreover, both Smith and Marx were in agreement with modern public opinion when they despised unproductive labor as parasitical, actually a kind of perversion of labor, as though nothing were worthy of this name which did not enrich the world. Marx certainly shared Smith’s contempt for the “menial servants” who like “idle guests . . . leave nothing behind them in return for their consumption.”

claims.claim: The productivity of labor power lies not in durable external products but in the human power to produce a surplus beyond what is required for its own reproduction.
claims.supporting_excerpt: This productivity does not lie in any of labor’s products but in the human “power,” whose strength is not exhausted when it has produced the means of its own subsistence and survival but is capable of producing a “surplus,” that is, more than is necessary for its own “reproduction.”

definitions.definition: A human power whose strength is not exhausted by producing the means of its own subsistence and is capable of producing a surplus beyond its own reproduction.

distinctions.distinction: Modern public opinion, Smith, and Marx traditionally separated them by viewing unproductive labor as parasitical and leaving nothing behind, whereas pre-modern ages identified the laboring condition of household servants (needed for consumption and subsistence) with slavery because it secured masters' freedom.

The productivity of work adds new objects to the human artifice, whereas the productivity of labor power produces objects only incidentally and is primarily concerned with the means of its own reproduction and life process.

must_not_be_lost: The distinction between productive and unproductive labor contains the more fundamental distinction between work and labor.
Marx's introduction of labor power as capable of a surplus was viewed by Engels as the most original and revolutionary element of his system.
output.segment_function: Examine the classical and Marxist distinction between productive and unproductive labor, the reinterpretation of labor power and its surplus, and the modern tendency to collapse labor into work within the perspective of the life process.
